title: The Essential Expedient Dharma-Gate of the Fourth Patriarch for Entering the Way and Settling the Mind (Selected Annotations)
author: One-Practice Samadhi
excerpt: Written by Daoxin, the Fourth Patriarch of Chan. The original text is recorded in the Record of the Masters and Disciples of the Lankavatara. Annotated by Zhanran.

blocks.text: The Essential Expedient Dharma-Gate of Entering the Way and Settling the Mind (Selected Annotations)

inline.s: Written by Daoxin, the Fourth Patriarch of Chan
The original text is recorded in the Record of the Masters and Disciples of the Lankavatara
Annotated by Zhanran
The realm of dharmas is a single mark; tie the mind to this realm of dharmas;
Do not seize upon marks, and remain unmoved in thusness.

The Essential Expedient Dharma-Gate of Entering the Way and Settling the Mind is divided into three parts: the main body, the questions and answers, and the miscellaneous records. This text annotates the main body. For readers unfamiliar with the reality of dharmas, it is suggested that you first read the
Reality of Dharmas
article.

For ease of reading and understanding, the renderings in the annotations are also set in quotation marks; but what lies within the quotation marks is not the original text — readers, please take note.

The Essential Expedient Dharma-Gate of Entering the Way and Settling the Mind”, that is: the essential expedient Dharma-gate for entering the Way and settling the mind. This is the instruction of Master Daoxin, the Fourth Patriarch of Chan — the essential gate that causes the mind to be calm and still, and so realize the undefiled holy Way.
[Daoxin (

)] his secular surname was Sima; he was born in Yongning County (today Meichuan Town, Wuxue City, Hubei Province), a great monk of the Sui and Tang, and the Fourth Patriarch of Chan. In the twelfth year of Kaihuang (
), he sought the Dharma from Sengcan, the Third Patriarch of Chan, and later received the precepts at Fu Temple in Jizhou. At age
he was entrusted with the robe and bowl by the Third Patriarch. In the eighth year of Wude (

), Master Daoxin preached and taught at the Temple of True Awakening on Mount Pofeng in Huangmei. When Emperor Taizong of Tang heard of the master’s style, he issued three edicts summoning him to the capital, but each time the master submitted a memorial declining to go. On the fourth sending, the emperor said: ‘If he still does not rise (if he still will not set out for the capital), then bring back his head.’ When the envoy reached the mountain and conveyed the emperor’s will, the master stretched out his neck to await the blade, his countenance grave and composed. The envoy, with no recourse, returned to the capital to report. The emperor admired him all the more and bestowed upon him a purple robe. In the eighteenth year of Zhenguan (
), he transmitted the Dharma to Hongren (the Fifth Patriarch of Chan), and in the second year of Yonghui (
), he passed away seated.
[Yanran] a grave and dignified countenance.
[Entering the Way] realizing the undefiled holy Way.

[Undefiled] pure, free of afflictions. ‘Defilement’ (lou) is another name for affliction — the sense of leaking out: the afflictions of greed, anger, and delusion flow and pour out ceaselessly day and night through the six sense-gates (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, mind), and this is called defilement. ‘Defilement’ also has the sense of falling: afflictions cause beings to fall into the three evil paths (hells, hungry ghosts, animals), and this is called defilement. To have afflictions is to be defiled; to be free of afflictions is to be undefiled. [Settling the mind] causing the mind to be calm and still. [Expedient] the means, methods, or words employed to guide and edify living beings; ‘expedient’ is spoken in contrast to ‘reality.’ [Reality] the actual state of things. The Sutra on the Treasury of the Buddha says:
“What is called the reality of all dharmas? That is to say, all dharmas are ultimately empty, without anything at all.”
As for the reality of dharmas, see in detail the
Reality of Dharmas
article.
[Record of the Masters and Disciples of the Lankavatara] one scroll in all. Compiled by Jingjue of the Tang dynasty (a disciple of Shenxiu of the Northern school) in the second year of Jinglong (

), it is also called the Record of the Lineage of the Masters and Disciples of the Lankavatara. This book recounts the transmission of the Lankavatara Sutra through eight generations. In the early period of Chan in China there was already a division between the Southern and Northern schools, and each school’s history of transmission regarded its own lineage as orthodox. This book takes the line of Shenxiu as the orthodox line of Chan and sets forth the lineage (transmission history) of the Northern school. Because the early masters especially emphasized the Lankavatara Sutra in their teaching, it is named the Record of the Masters and Disciples of the Lankavatara. Its contents run in this order: (1) Gunabhadra, the translator of the Lankavatara Sutra; (2) Bodhidharma (Patriarch Bodhidharma); (3) Huike; (4) Sengcan; (5) Daoxin; (6) Hongren; (7) Shenxiu, Xuanze (
zé
), and Lao’an; (8) Puji, Jingxian, Yifu, Huifu, and others — the transmission of eight generations. All of the above belong to the Northern school system.
[Masters and disciples] teachers and students.

[Southern and Northern schools] From Bodhidharma, the First Patriarch, to Hongren, the Fifth Patriarch, Chan was one undivided flavor. Below Hongren were the two disciples Huineng and Shenxiu, who formed the Southern and Northern schools. Huineng’s style flourished in the south of the Yangtze, so it was called the Southern school; Shenxiu’s teaching flourished in the northern capital region, so it was called the Northern school. That which later flourished greatly was the Southern school.
[One flavor] sole and undivided.

[My essential Dharma rests upon the “Buddha-Mind Foremost” of the Lankavatara Sutra, and upon the One-Practice Samadhi of the Sutra of the Prajna Spoken by Manjushri — namely, the mind that recollects the Buddha is Buddha, and the mind of deluded thought is an ordinary being.]

This essential Dharma of entering the Way and settling the mind of mine is based upon the “Buddha-Mind Foremost” of the Lankavatara Sutra and upon the One-Practice Samadhi of the Sutra of the Prajna Spoken by Manjushri, namely: the mind that recollects the Buddha is Buddha, and the mind of deluded thought is an ordinary being.
[Buddha-Mind Foremost] The Lankavatara Sutra says:
“Among the various gates of liberation of the Great Vehicle, the mind of the Buddhas is foremost.”

[Among the various gates of liberation of the Great Vehicle, the mind of the Buddhas is foremost] Among the many Dharma-gates of liberation of the Great Vehicle, the mind of the Buddhas is the first Dharma-gate — the gate of no marks.
(See in detail the
Selections from the Lankavatara Sutra
.) [The mind of the Buddhas] this refers to the still and clear mind spoken of further on. In the Sutra on the Treasury of the Buddha, the Buddha says:
“The anuttara-samyak-sambodhi of all the Buddhas is entirely without thought and without ideation.”
[Sutra of the Prajna Spoken by Manjushri] its full name is the Maha-prajnaparamita Sutra Spoken by Manjushri.

[One-Practice Samadhi] settling the mind on a single practice and cultivating samadhi (right concentration). The Enumeration of the Dharmas of the Three Treasuries says: “One-Practice Samadhi is the practice of concentrating solely on one practice, cultivating right concentration.”

[The Sutra of the Prajna Spoken by Manjushri says: “Manjushri said: World-Honored One, what is called One-Practice Samadhi? The Buddha said: The realm of dharmas is a single mark; tie the mind to this realm of dharmas — this is called One-Practice Samadhi.”]

The Sutra of the Prajna Spoken by Manjushri says: “Manjushri Bodhisattva asked: World-Honored One, what is One-Practice Samadhi? The Buddha replied: The realm of dharmas is a single mark; tie the mind to this single-marked realm of dharmas — this is called One-Practice Samadhi.”
Therefore, One-Practice Samadhi is the tying of the mind to the single-marked realm of dharmas (the noumenal dharma-realm).

[Dharma-realm] In terms of phenomenal marks, ‘dharmas’ are the various dharmas and ‘realm’ is their demarcation; all things in the phenomenal world each bear distinct, different marks that cannot be confused, and this is called the ‘phenomenal dharma-realm.’ In terms of noumenal essence, though dharmas differ in outer marks, they all share the same inner nature, and this is called the ‘noumenal dharma-realm.’ [The realm of dharmas is a single mark] the single-marked realm of dharmas — this is the noumenal dharma-realm. The Sutra on the Treasury of the Buddha says:
“All the marks of dharmas are a single mark, namely no-mark.”
(Translation: the marks of all dharmas are in fact the same single mark, and this ‘mark’ is: nothing.) See in detail the
Selections from the Sutra on the Treasury of the Buddha

. [Nothing] Worldly speech says: a cow has horns, a rabbit has no horns. The ‘nothing’ they speak of is spoken in contrast to ‘something.’ But the ‘nothing’ of the ‘single mark’ here transcends the nothing and something of worldly speech; it is the ‘nothing’ of which the Sixth Patriarch Huineng spoke, “originally there was not a single thing.” (See in detail
A Detailed Explanation of the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch
.) [The realm of dharmas is a single mark; tie the mind to this realm of dharmas] this is tying the mind to the noumenal dharma-realm.
The passage in which the World-Honored One answers Manjushri Bodhisattva is:

“The realm of dharmas is a single mark; tie the mind to this realm of dharmas — this is called One-Practice Samadhi. If good men and good women wish to enter One-Practice Samadhi, they should first hear the Prajna-paramita, study and cultivate in accordance with the teaching, and then they can enter One-Practice Samadhi, tying the mind to the realm of dharmas, non-retreating and indestructible, inconceivable, unobstructed and without mark. Good men and good women who wish to enter One-Practice Samadhi should dwell in a quiet place, abandon all distractions, not seize upon appearances, fix the mind on a single Buddha, single-mindedly call upon his name, and in accord with the direction where that Buddha dwells, straighten the body and face towards it. Being able to continue thought after thought on one Buddha — in that very thought they see the Buddhas of the past, future, and present. Why is that? The merit of recollecting a single Buddha is immeasurable and boundless, and is no different from the merit of the immeasurable Buddhas. The inconceivable Buddha-dharmas are equally without distinction; all ride upon the one Thusness and accomplish the utmost right awakening, fully endowed with immeasurable merit and immeasurable eloquence. Those who thus enter One-Practice Samadhi fully know the Dharma-realms of the Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, without a differing mark.”

From this passage it can be known: tying the mind to the single-marked realm of dharmas is One-Practice Samadhi. And studying and cultivating the Prajna scriptures is the theoretical foundation for entering One-Practice Samadhi; the mind-fixing Buddha-recollection that does not seize upon appearances and single-mindedly calls upon the name is the path for entering One-Practice Samadhi. When the mind of thought after thought ‘suddenly becomes still and clear, with nothing further to be mindful of,’ one enters One-Practice Samadhi.
In the Record of the Masters and Disciples of the Lankavatara, there is this account:
“In the first year of Dazu (
(Master Shenxiu)

was summoned to the Eastern Capital and, accompanying the imperial carriage, went back and forth between the two capitals in teaching, personally serving as teacher to the emperor. Empress Zetian of the Great Sage asked Chan Master Shenxiu: ‘The Dharma you transmit — of whose school is the teaching?’ He replied: ‘I inherit the Dongshan Dharma-gate of
Qizhou

.’ She asked: ‘Which text does it rely upon?’ He replied: ‘It relies upon the One-Practice Samadhi of the Sutra of the Prajna Spoken by Manjushri.’ Zetian said: ‘If we speak of cultivating the Way, nothing surpasses the Dongshan Dharma-gate.’”
Translation: In the first year of Dazu (

), Master Shenxiu, summoned to the Eastern Capital (Luoyang), accompanied the imperial carriage back and forth between the two capitals (the Western Capital Chang’an and the Eastern Capital Luoyang) in teaching, personally serving as teacher to the three emperors (Wu Zetian, Zhongzong, and Ruizong of the Tang). Wu Zetian asked Master Shenxiu: ‘The Dharma you transmit — of whose school is the teaching?’ Master Shenxiu replied: ‘I inherit the Dongshan Dharma-gate of Master Hongren of Qizhou.’ Wu Zetian asked: ‘Which scripture does it rely upon?’ Shenxiu replied: ‘It relies upon the One-Practice Samadhi in the Sutra of the Prajna Spoken by Manjushri.’ Zetian said: ‘If we speak of cultivating the Way, nothing is higher than the Dongshan Dharma-gate.’
From this exchange, we can see that the One-Practice Samadhi of the Sutra of the Prajna Spoken by Manjushri is extremely important.

[If good men and good women wish to enter One-Practice Samadhi, they should first hear the Prajna-paramita, study and cultivate in accordance with the teaching, and then they can enter One-Practice Samadhi, tying the mind to the realm of dharmas, non-retreating and indestructible, inconceivable, unobstructed and without mark.]

If good men and good women wish to enter One-Practice Samadhi, they should first read the Prajna scriptures, study and cultivate in accordance with the teaching, and then they can enter One-Practice Samadhi, tying the mind unmoved in thusness to the single-marked realm of dharmas — non-retreating and indestructible, inconceivable, unobstructed and without mark.
In this passage, the World-Honored One reveals: studying and cultivating the Prajna scriptures is the theoretical foundation for entering One-Practice Samadhi.

[Prajna-paramita] crossing, with the wonderful wisdom of prajna, to the shore of nirvana (attaining Buddhahood). ‘Prajna’ is a transliteration of Sanskrit and means wisdom, but this wisdom is not the cleverness of the world; rather, it is the wonderful wisdom that penetrates the true reality of life and the universe (the reality of dharmas), omniscient and omnipotent, the right wisdom of self-nature. The Treatise on the Great Perfection of Wisdom says:
“Prajna is the mother of all the Buddhas; dwelling in this prajna, one is able to fully realize all the Buddha-dharmas.”

‘Paramita’ is a transliteration of Sanskrit, also rendered paramita-multiplied — meaning: reaching the other shore. We ordinary beings, from beginningless time onward, have drifted in the sea of karma, now emerging and now submerged. To study Buddhism is to cross this sea of birth-and-death, where the winds of conditions howl and the waves of consciousness surge, and reach the shore of ultimate nirvana. The Treatise on the Great Perfection of Wisdom says:
“Prajna-paramita is the mother of all the Buddhas. All the Buddhas take the Dharma as their teacher. The Dharma is precisely prajna-paramita.”
The Great Prajna Sutra says:
“Maha-prajna-paramita is the mother of all great bodhisattvas; it gives birth to all the Buddhas and embraces the bodhisattvas.”

[Prajna scriptures] a general name for the scriptures that expound the profound principle of prajna-paramita — for example, the Large Prajna Sutra, the Small Prajna Sutra, the Great Prajna Sutra, the Prajna-paramita Heart Sutra (that is, the Heart Sutra — see in detail the
A Detailed Explanation of the Heart Sutra
), the Vajra-prajna-paramita Sutra (that is, the Diamond Sutra — see in detail the
A Detailed Explanation of the Diamond Sutra
), and others.

[Good men and good women who wish to enter One-Practice Samadhi should dwell in a quiet place, abandon all distractions, not seize upon appearances, fix the mind on a single Buddha, single-mindedly call upon his name, and in accord with the direction where that Buddha dwells, straighten the body and face towards it. Being able to continue thought after thought on one Buddha — in that very thought they see the Buddhas of the past, future, and present.]

Good men and good women who wish to enter One-Practice Samadhi should, in a quiet place, rid themselves of delusive thought (abandon all distractions), and without seizing upon appearances, fix the mind on a single Buddha, single-mindedly call upon his name, and in accord with the direction where that Buddha dwells, straighten the body and face towards it. Being able to call continuously, thought after thought, on one Buddha — in that very thought they see the Buddhas of the past, future, and present.
[Thought-after-thought continuation]
the thought of Buddha-recollection continuing on, unbroken by delusive thoughts.

The key to “fixing the mind on a single Buddha and single-mindedly calling upon his name” is to achieve thought-after-thought continuation — that is, the “pure thought following one after another” spoken of in the Chapter on the Perfect Penetration of the Buddha-Recollection of Bodhisattva Mahasthamaprapta; this is the state in which all thoughts return to the one.

In this passage, the World-Honored One reveals: mind-fixing Buddha-recollection, done without seizing upon appearances and calling single-mindedly upon the name, is the path for entering One-Practice Samadhi. On how to recollect the Buddha, see in detail
The Awareness of Buddha-Recollection

[Why is that? The merit of recollecting a single Buddha is immeasurable and boundless, and is no different from the merit of the immeasurable Buddhas. The inconceivable Buddha-dharmas are equally without distinction; all ride upon the one Thusness and accomplish the utmost right awakening, fully endowed with immeasurable merit and immeasurable eloquence. Those who thus enter One-Practice Samadhi fully know the Dharma-realms of the Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, without a differing mark.”]

Why is that? The merit of recollecting a single Buddha is immeasurable and boundless, and is no different from the merit of recollecting the immeasurable Buddhas. The inconceivable Buddha-dharmas are equally without distinction; all ride upon the one Thusness and accomplish the utmost right awakening (attain Buddhahood), fully endowed with immeasurable merit and immeasurable eloquence. Those who thus enter One-Practice Samadhi fully know the Dharma-realms of the Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, without a differing mark.’”
[One-Thusness] non-dual and non-different is called one-Thusness, that is, the principle of true thusness.
The scripture passages quoted in this text end here; what follows is the discourse of the Fourth Patriarch.
[Now, the body and mind within this square inch — every lifting of the foot and setting it down — are always in the practice ground; all one’s actions and movements are bodhi.]

One who wishes to enter One-Practice Samadhi should — in body (conduct) and mind (thought), in every lifting of the foot and setting it down — always dwell in the practice ground, and all one’s actions and movements should be in awareness (rather than unconscious).
[Fu] a classical particle opening the sentence. [Square inch] refers to a person’s innermost mind. Master Daoxin said:

“The hundreds and thousands of Dharma-gates all return to this square inch; the wonderful virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges all lie in the source of the mind. The gate of precepts, the gate of concentration, the gate of wisdom, and spiritual powers and transformations — all are fully present, never apart from your mind.”
(The Essentials of the Five Lamps)
[Source of the mind] because the mind is the source of all dharmas, it is called the source of the mind. The Treatise on the Bodhi-Mind says:

“If the deluded mind arises, know it and do not follow it. When delusion subsides, the source of the mind is empty and still. All virtues are complete, and the wonderful functioning is inexhaustible.”
[Practice ground] the place where one cultivates and realizes the Way. [Bodhi] in Chinese it is translated as ‘awakening.’

[All in awareness] There is this story: it is said that a fly came and alighted upon the Buddha’s face, and the Buddha gently waved it away with his hand; then he made a waving gesture a second time. A disciple, puzzled, asked: ‘World-Honored One, the first time you waved was to drive away the fly, and the second time — what was that for?’ The Buddha replied: ‘The first was an unconscious action, done without awareness; so I performed the second with awareness, to correct it.’ This manifestation of the Buddha teaches us: every action should be clearly known; an action without awareness is ignorance and should be corrected at once.
As practice deepens, karmic hindrances often entangle one. Here the Fourth Patriarch especially reveals the foremost repentance for removing karmic hindrances — the repentance of reality.

[The Sutra of the Contemplation of Universal Good says: “The ocean of all karmic hindrances is born of delusive thought; if one wishes to repent, sit upright and contemplate reality.” This is called the foremost repentance.]

The Sutra of the Contemplation of Universal Good (full name: The Sutra of the Dharma of Contemplating the Practice of Bodhisattva Universal Good) says: “The ocean of all karmic hindrances is born of delusive thought; if one wishes to repent, sit upright and contemplate reality.” To sit upright and contemplate reality — this is the foremost repentance.
The Sutra of the Dharma of Contemplating the Practice of Bodhisattva Universal Good says:
“The ocean of all karmic hindrances is born of delusive thought. If one wishes to repent, sit upright and contemplate reality. All offenses are like frost and dew, and the sun of wisdom (
contemplating reality
) can melt them away.”

[The ocean of all karmic hindrances is born of delusive thought; if one wishes to repent, sit upright and contemplate reality] All karmic hindrances, as deep and vast as the sea, are born of delusive thought; if one wishes to repent, sit upright and contemplate reality. Therefore, sitting upright and contemplating reality can wipe away all karmic hindrances. [Contemplating reality] the mind that has no object (without thought, without ideation) — this is contemplating reality. (See in detail the section “the sun of wisdom wipes away offenses” in the
Essentials of Chan and Pure Land

[Set aside the mind of the three poisons and the mind of clinging, and with a mind that observes with awareness recollect the Buddha, thought following thought. Suddenly it becomes still and clear, with nothing further to be mindful of. The Large Sutra says: “To have nothing to think of — this is called recollecting the Buddha.” What is “nothing to think of”? That is, the mind that recollects the Buddha is called “nothing to think of.” Apart from the mind there is no other Buddha; apart from the Buddha there is no other mind. To recollect the Buddha is to recollect the mind; to seek the mind is to seek the Buddha.]

Set aside the mind of the three poisons (greed, anger, and delusion) and the mind of clinging, and with a mind that observes the present thought with awareness recollect the Buddha, thought following thought (without mixing in delusive thoughts). As the practice deepens over time, suddenly it becomes still and clear (the very thought of recollecting the Buddha also subsides), with nothing further to be mindful of. This is what the Large Prajna Sutra says:
“To have nothing to think of — this is called recollecting the Buddha.”

What is called “nothing to think of”? That is, this still and clear mind of recollecting the Buddha is called “nothing to think of.” Apart from this still and clear mind there is no other Buddha; apart from the Buddha there is no other such still and clear mind. To recollect the Buddha is to recollect this still and clear mind; to seek this still and clear mind is to seek the Buddha.
Suddenly still and clear, with nothing further to be mindful of”:

suddenly one day, without calling the Buddha’s name and without delusive thoughts. This is the state of passing from the many thoughts returning to the one, and then the one returning to nothing — what the Pure Land school calls “recollection without remembering, remembering without recollection”; what the Large Prajna Sutra says:
“To have nothing to think of — this is called recollecting the Buddha.”

At this time, with nothing further to be mindful of, one enters the One-Practice Samadhi of the Sutra of the Prajna Spoken by Manjushri. This state is what, at the very beginning of this text, was called “the mind that recollects the Buddha is Buddha.”

[Mind that observes with awareness] the mind of clear awareness and observation. Here “awareness and observation” does not have the sense of the earlier-search-and-reflection. [Mind of clinging] the mind that clings to the six sense-objects (forms, sounds, scents, tastes, tangibles, and dharmas). Setting aside the mind of clinging is to not seize upon marks and to remain unmoved in thusness. The Diamond Sutra says:
“All marks whatsoever are false and vain.” “Not seizing upon marks, remaining unmoved in thusness.”

[Large Sutra] that is, the Large Prajna Sutra. The Maha-prajnaparamita Sutra translated by Kumarajiva exists in a twenty-seven-roll version and a ten-roll version; the former is called the “Large Prajna Sutra” and the latter the “Small Prajna Sutra.” The full name of the six-hundred-roll Prajna Sutra translated by Master Xuanzang is the Great Prajna-paramita Sutra.
[To have nothing to think of — this is called recollecting the Buddha] This is what is commonly called “recollection without remembering, remembering without recollection.” The Buddha says:

“Shariputra, what is called recollecting the Buddha? Seeing that there is nothing at all is called recollecting the Buddha. Shariputra, the Buddhas are immeasurable, inconceivable, and beyond weighing; for this reason, seeing that there is nothing at all is called recollecting the Buddha. Reality is without discrimination, and the Buddhas are without discrimination; therefore it is said that recollecting without discrimination is recollecting the Buddha. Seeing the reality of all dharmas is called seeing the Buddha. What is called the reality of all dharmas? That is to say, all dharmas are ultimately empty, without anything at all. Because of this reality that is ultimately empty and without anything, one recollects the Buddha. Furthermore, in such dharmas, even a single small thought cannot be obtained — this is called recollecting the Buddha. Shariputra, this Dharma of recollecting the Buddha cuts off the path of speech, passes beyond all thoughts; it cannot be caught by thought — this is called recollecting the Buddha. Shariputra, all thoughts bear the mark of extinction; following along with this Dharma is called cultivating Buddha-recollection. One cannot recollect the Buddha by form; why? To think of form is to seize upon a mark, and to savor its flavor is consciousness. Without form, without color, without condition, without nature — this is called recollecting the Buddha. Therefore know: without discrimination, without grasping and without renouncing — this is true recollecting the Buddha.”
(The Sutra on the Treasury of the Buddha)
[Why is this so? Consciousness is formless; the Buddha is formless; the Buddha has no appearance. If one also realizes this truth, this is “settling the mind.”]
Why? Because consciousness is formless, the Buddha is formless, and the Buddha has no appearance. If one actually realizes this truth, this is “settling the mind.”
[If one also realizes this truth] The Treatise on Extinction of Contemplation says:
“A question: since it is said that emptiness is the root of the Way, is emptiness the Buddha? Answer: it is so (
this is so
). Question: if emptiness is the case (
if emptiness is the Buddha

), why do the sages not cause beings to recollect emptiness, but cause them to recollect the Buddha? Answer: for foolish beings one teaches them to recollect the Buddha; if there are those of the Way-mind, one causes them to contemplate the reality of the body, and to contemplate the Buddha likewise. Now, what is called reality is precisely the empty and markless.”

[This is “settling the mind”] “The wild mind does not rest; when it rests, that is bodhi.” The reason beings’ wild mind does not rest is that they falsely cling to the dharmas as real, pursuing and grasping without satiety, thoughts flying in all directions. If one truly understands the truth of the reality of all dharmas, what is there to grasp? What is there to think of? Then the mind is naturally without thought, and so it comes to rest. Elder Xuyun instructs:
“Only because
(simply because)

you and I, from countless kalpas on, have been deluded and sunk in birth-and-death, defiled for so long that we cannot at once cast off delusive thoughts and truly see the original nature — therefore one must practice Chan. Hence the prerequisite for practicing Chan is to remove delusive thoughts. How are delusive thoughts removed? The Buddha Shakyamuni spoke much on this; the simplest is the single word ‘rest’ in ‘when [the mind] rests, that is bodhi.’”
(The Convenient Instructions of Elder Xuyun
The Prerequisite for Practicing Chan)

[Always recollect the Buddha, and clinging does not arise; then all is stilled into the markless, equal and non-dual. Entering this stage, the recollection-mind fades away, and there is no need to call it forth again.]

Always recollect the Buddha in this way (“to have nothing to think of — this is called recollecting the Buddha”), and clinging does not arise; then the distinctions among dharmas vanish completely and return to the markless, and all dharmas are equal, non-dual. Entering this markless stage, the mind that recollects the Buddha without thought fades away (the recollection-mind fades), and there is no need to call it forth again.
[Equal, non-dual] Viewed in the light of the reality of all dharmas, all dharmas have no mutual distinctions and are entirely equal. The Heart Sutra says:
“These dharmas are of empty mark — not born, not destroyed, not defiled, not pure, not increased, not decreased.”
(Translation: these dharmas are phantoms; in reality there is no birth and no extinction, no defilement and no purity, no increase and no decrease. See in detail the
A Detailed Explanation of the Heart Sutra
.) [The reality of all dharmas] the actual state of all dharmas. In the Sutra on the Treasury of the Buddha
Chapter Two on the Buddha-Recollection, the Buddha says:
“What is called the reality of all dharmas? That is to say, all dharmas are ultimately empty, without anything at all.”
In the Great Parinirvana Sutra, the Buddha says:
“All dharmas whatsoever are false and vain.”
In the Sutra of Upholding the World, the Buddha says:
“Know that all dharmas are empty, like an illusion without reality, with no root.”
(For a detailed discussion of the reality of all dharmas, see the
Reality of Dharmas
article.) [The recollection-mind fades away]
the mind that recollects the Buddha without thought fades and vanishes,

entering the state in which there is neither an observer nor an object observed. This is what Chan calls “the void shattering, the great earth sinking away, the body, mind, and world fading and vanishing” — the state of personally witnessing the original nature. [Sinking away] disappearing, vanishing.
Chan Master Baizhang, ascending the hall, said:

“The spiritual light shines alone, utterly freed from the sense-bases and sense-objects. The essence is revealed as true and eternal, not confined by words. The mind-nature is undefiled, originally complete and perfect. Only cast off the false clinging, and you are the Buddha in thusness.”
(The Essentials of the Five Lamps)

[False clinging] clinging of one’s own making; here “cling” is a verb. [Only cast off the false clinging, and you are the Buddha in thusness] As soon as one casts off clinging of one’s own making, one is the Dharmakaya Buddha. The Lankavatara Sutra says:
“The Dharma Buddha (
the Dharmakaya Buddha
) is one who is free from clinging.”
The Diamond Sutra says:
“One who is free from all marks is called a Buddha.”
[Buddha in thusness] the Buddha who awakens to the essence of thusness, that is, the Dharmakaya Buddha. The Lankavatara Sutra says:
“What is the transformational Buddha? What is the reward Buddha? What is the Buddha in thusness?”
Master Hanshan said:

“When you see the place where a single thought does not arise, then the frontier of the past and the frontier of the future are cut off, and the middle stands alone. Suddenly the lacquer bucket is broken through, and you abruptly see your original face. Then the body, mind, and world at once sink away, like an empty flower shadowed and falling; the ten quarters are perfectly luminous, becoming one great treasury of light. Only then is it the time of arriving home; it is present in daily use, bright and perfectly round, with nothing more to doubt. Then for the first time you believe your mind is originally like this. The Buddhas and Patriarchs of old, in their own enjoyment, are no different from this, not two, not other.”
The Dream Roaming Collection
On the Essentials of Recollecting the Buddha and Practicing Chan

[The frontier of the past and the frontier of the future] the past frontier refers to the past, and the future frontier refers to the future. The Commentary on the Pure Land [or the Commentary on the Flower Adornment] says: “Conditioned dharmas arise one after another, past and future; the former is the past frontier, the latter the future frontier.” [The frontier of the past and the future are cut off] no past thought and no future thought, that is, the state in which a single thought does not arise. The Mirror of the Source:

“Therefore the Essentials of the Mind says: if a single thought does not arise, then the frontier of the past and the frontier of the future are cut off. The radiant essence stands alone, both things and self are in thusness, and one goes straight to the source of the mind.”
The General Preface to the Collected Commentaries on the Sources of Chan says:
“On hearing one, one awakens to a thousand; one attains the great total upholding. When a single thought does not arise, the frontier of the past and the frontier of the future are cut off.”
[Sinking away]
also written “sinking down”: disappearing, vanishing.

[Just look at this mind, and it is the body of the Tathagata’s true Dharma-nature; it is also called the right Dharma, also called Buddha-nature, also called the real nature and actual reality of all dharmas, also called the Pure Land, also called bodhi, the vajra-samadhi, the original awakening, and others; also called the realm of nirvana, prajna, and others. Though the names are immeasurable, they all are one body; there is also no intent of an observer and an observed.]

Just look at this mind, and it is the Dharmakaya of the Tathagata; it is also called the right Dharma, also called Buddha-nature, also called the real nature and actual reality of all dharmas, also called the Pure Land, also called bodhi, the vajra-samadhi, the original awakening, and others; also called the realm of nirvana, prajna, and others. Though the names are immeasurable and countless, they all speak of the same one thing, that is, the intent of no observer and no observed.

[The body of Dharma-nature] Also called the Dharma-body, the true body of the Buddha. [No one who contemplates, no object contemplated] There is no mind that contemplates and no realm that is contemplated
. This is the state in which subject and object both vanish and one personally realizes the nature

[These very kinds of mind one must cause to be pure and eternally present before one, so that all the various conditions cannot disturb or confuse them. Why? Because all the various things are all the one Dharma-body of the Tathagata. Dwelling in this mind, the various bonds and afflictions are naturally extinguished.]

These very kinds of mind (that is, the 'these kinds of mind' spoken of above) must be kept pure and eternally present before one (this is the work of nurturing and maintaining after the realization of the nature); then all the various conditions are unable to disturb or confuse. Why? Because within such a mind all things and affairs are all the one Dharma-body of the Tathagata. Dwelling in such a mind, the many kinds of affliction are naturally extinguished.
[All things are the one Dharma-body of the Tathagata] For this principle, see in detail
Mind, Self-Nature, and the Tathagatagarbha
The True Reality of All Dharmas
. [Bond]

The meaning of binding together and of tying down; a different name for the afflictions. Because afflictions, as cause, bind together birth-and-death, they are called bonds; and because they bind living beings and do not allow them release, they too are called bonds.
If greed, anger, or delusion arises, immediately fix the attention upon 'these very kinds of mind,' and greed, anger, and delusion will at once lose their power.

[Within a single mote of dust are contained measureless worlds; measureless worlds gather upon the tip of a single hair. Their original nature being thus, they do not hinder one another. The Avatamsaka Sutra says: 'There is a scroll of scripture within a mote of dust, wherein one sees the affairs of the three thousand great thousand realms.']

Realize that within a single mote of dust are contained measureless worlds, and that measureless worlds gather upon the tip of a single hair. Because their original nature (the original matter, that is, the true face of all dharmas) is thus, they do not hinder one another. The Avatamsaka Sutra says: 'There is a scroll of scripture within a mote of dust, wherein one sees the affairs of the three thousand great thousand realms.'

[The character 'thus' (ru)] Its meaning is: things are the same as one another, ever constant and unchanging. Here it refers to the true, unchanging nature of all things. This nature is extremely hard to describe in words and sentences, so the character 'thus' is borrowed to stand for it. The nature is reality, and reality is thus, because it is not two, is not altered, does not change, and does not move. The true face of all dharmas is in every case this single same mark, and so it is called 'thus.'

[Within a mote of dust, one sees the affairs of the three thousand great thousand realms] This teaches the Avatamsaka's realm of unimpeded interpenetration among phenomena: in each mote of dust are all Buddha-lands, and within each of those Buddha-lands there are countless motes of dust, and each of these motes again contains all Buddha-lands, layer upon layer without end. [The realm of unimpeded interpenetration among phenomena] One of the four dharma-realms. [The four dharma-realms] The dharma-realm of phenomena, the dharma-realm of principle, the dharma-realm of the unimpeded interpenetration of principle and phenomena, and the dharma-realm of the unimpeded interpenetration among phenomena. The differing marks of all the dharmas of the world, each distinct and not to be confused, are called the dharma-realm of phenomena; the principle-substance of suchness, equal and single, on which all dharmas rely, is called the dharma-realm of principle; because suchness can give rise to all dharmas, all dharmas are suchness, and the principle-substance and the phenomenal marks interpenetrate and mutually possess one another, passing without obstruction, so that principle is phenomena and phenomena are principle, and this is called the dharma-realm of the unimpeded interpenetration of principle and phenomena; all dharmas mutually encompass one another, layer upon layer without end, without obstructing one another, one and many being identical, great and small mutually containing one another, one taken up and all received, fully corresponding, and this is called the dharma-realm of the unimpeded interpenetration among phenomena. [Layer upon layer without end] Taking dust-motes and Buddha-lands as an example, each mote of dust contains all Buddha-lands, and within each of those Buddha-lands there are countless motes of dust, and each of these motes again contains all Buddha-lands, and so on ad infinitum: dust contains lands, and lands again contain dust, one layer following another without end, and so it is called layer upon layer without end.
[Briefly setting forth the settling of the mind, it cannot be exhausted in full; the skillful means within it issue from the square inch of the heart.]

The above is but a brief account of this method of settling the mind, 'the single mark of the dharma-realm, tethering the mind to the dharma-realm.' This method is deep and vast without end, and it is impossible to set it all forth point by point; the skillful means within it reside in the one mind.
Break existence, extinguish feeling, cut off deliberation, leave suffering
To cling to existence is to give rise to feeling; the three poisons
(greed, anger, delusion)
swarm up, and day and night one is anxious and tormented by suffering.
When existence is broken, feeling perishes; when feeling perishes, deliberation is cut off; when deliberation is cut off, one leaves suffering and crosses beyond every suffering and distress.
If there is deliberation, then feeling has not perished; if feeling remains, then existence has not been broken.
That originally there is nothing the matter is awakening; extinguishing feeling and cutting off deliberation is cultivation.
Though one has this wisdom that is able to comprehend, it too is like the mind of a dream,
even were there to be a single dharma surpassing nirvana, it too would be like a dream, like an illusion.

The essential expedient gate of entering the Way and settling the mind is this: the single mark of the dharma-realm, tethering the mind to the dharma-realm; without grasping at marks, abiding in immovable suchness.
(Tethered to the dharma-realm of principle, with regard to the various dharmas of the dharma-realm of phenomena one does not grasp at marks and abides in immovable suchness.)

[The single mark of the dharma-realm, tethering the mind to the dharma-realm] This is tethering the mind to the dharma-realm of principle. [Without grasping at marks, abiding in immovable suchness] With regard to the various dharmas of the dharma-realm of phenomena, one does not grasp at marks and abides in immovable suchness. The Diamond Sutra says:
"All marks whatsoever are all illusory."

'Without grasping at marks, abiding in immovable suchness' means not to hold marks to be real and be drawn about by them. That is to say, not to be attached to marks, and not to move the mind. [Ruru] The first 'ru' means 'as' or 'like'; the second 'ru' is suchness (the nature). 'Ruru' thus means 'like suchness': this is the state of immobility, of quiescence, of equal non-duality, and of freedom from inverted discrimination. [Quiescence] To have no affliction is called 'quiescence' (ji); to have no birth-and-death is called 'extinction' (mie); the state in which there is no affliction and no birth-and-death is nirvana.
The above teaching has three levels:
1. Thought after thought continuing, this is the state in which the ten thousand thoughts return to one
(only the thought of reciting the Buddha-name)
2. Suddenly clear and still, this is the state in which the one returns to nothing
(no-thought)
3. The recollection of the Buddha fades away, this is the state in which subject and object both vanish and one personally realizes the nature.
[Both subject and object vanish] There is no mind that contemplates and no realm that is contemplated. For example, in the Chan practice of Xuyun (see
Awareness Chan

), one looks at what precedes the topic phrase: the moment a single thought arises, it has already become the tail of the phrase. Therefore, to be able to see what precedes the topic phrase is to be in the state of no-thought; but at this point there is still a mind that contemplates and a realm that is contemplated (that which precedes the topic phrase). And so one must, from the top of a hundred-foot pole, take one step further, and only then accomplish the vanishing of both subject and object and personally realize the nature.

The section 'Eternally Present Before One' speaks of the work of nurturing and maintaining after the realization of the nature. The central task of this nurturing and maintaining is to wash away habitual tendencies: cause 'these very kinds of mind' to be eternally present before one, and through fine and unbroken contemplation reduce the habits of greed, anger, and delusion further and further, until they come to nothing.

[Fine and unbroken contemplation] To practice again and again, finely and unceasingly, the work of 'when a thought arises, immediately be aware; when aware, it vanishes.' [When a thought arises, immediately be aware; when aware, it vanishes] If a false thought arises, one must immediately realize: this is taking an illusion for real, being turned about by illusory marks. Having become aware of this point, the false thought immediately vanishes. [Until they come to nothing] With regard to any thing at all of body, mind, or world, one no longer has greed, anger, or delusion.
Question:
The Sutra of the Buddha's Treasury says:
"The anuttara-samyak-sambodhi of all the Buddhas is entirely without thought, entirely without mind."
The Essentials of the Mind-Dharma Transmission says:
"Still thought and forget
(here the character is interchangeable in meaning with 'perish')
deliberation, and the Buddha appears of itself before you."
The Treatise on Abandoning Contemplation says:
"No-thought is no-mind; no-mind is the true Way."
How can one accomplish no-mind?
Answer: the single mark of the dharma-realm, tethering the mind to the dharma-realm; without grasping at marks, abiding in immovable suchness.
